genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure first held a junior post in a care establishment
an experienced colleague urged her to train
she studied in the evenings for three years before qualifying
she won the creation of a room set aside for movement by expectant mothers
her managers resisted the request at first
she passed her experience on to carers who came from distant districts
she still runs a training session now that her working life has ended
she holds that listening works as well as a drug treatment
text: The midwife at the valley clinic started out as a care assistant. She stripped beds, wheeled trolleys about and listened to women describe pains that nobody bothered to take seriously. An older nurse kept telling her she ought to train properly. So she took evening classes, and three years later she qualified. Once she joined the ward, she pushed for a room where expectant mothers could walk, breathe and doze between contractions. Her managers dug their heels in, then gave way. Later she taught carers who came from far-off districts, showing them the small handlings that no manual has ever set down. She retired not long ago, yet she still runs a workshop where young staff learn to listen before they reach for a prescription. Patience, she says, eases as much as a well-judged medicine.

units: the most striking feature of the establishment is how quiet it is
an absorbent covering muffles the sound of movement
visitors lower their voices without being asked
the writer holds that noise breeds tiredness
tiredness spoils the mood and works against falling asleep
removing the source of sound breaks that sequence
the writer finds the communal rooms and the cooking dull
after two nights the muscular tension eases
text: What stays with you about this rest centre is not the pale brickwork but the quiet it manufactures. The corridors are wide and lined with a thick felt, and that covering swallows every footstep so thoroughly that the ear finally lets go. The effect catches you out: guests who arrive wound tight begin to speak softly, though nobody has asked them to. The reason behind it is plain, almost mechanical. Noise tires you, tiredness sours the temper, and a soured temper keeps sleep at bay. Take away the first link and the whole chain falls apart. You could fault the communal rooms for their blandness and the kitchen for its timid cooking. Set against the result, such failings weigh very little. Two nights in, the shoulders drop, the jaw unclenches, and you catch yourself dozing in a chair without a shred of guilt.

units: the writer puts the night-time cough down to the state of the bedroom
the air in the room is too dry and is never renewed
dryness irritates the lining and sets off a cough
he advises opening the window before going to bed
he explains that cold air once warmed brings moisture
he recommends turning the heating down
he suggests standing a bowl of water near the source of heat
he proposes drinking enough during the evening
he asks for a nightly note of how the symptom changes
he invites a visit to a doctor if the attempt fails
text: I am writing because that night-time cough is robbing you of sleep, and I suspect the fault lies in your bedroom rather than in your chest. The air in there never moves: the window stays shut, the radiator runs on and on, and the moisture drops below any comfortable level. A dried-out lining grows irritated and answers with a dry cough, which starts up the moment you lie flat. Here is what I would have you try for a week. Open the window a quarter of an hour before bed, even in a hard frost; cold air, once warmed indoors, holds more vapour than stale air does. Then turn the heating down a notch and stand a bowl of water on the sill. Drink enough during the evening, without overdoing it. Note each night whether the cough returns. If nothing shifts after a week, see a doctor. I will come with you.

units: the question asked compares the value of running with that of brisk walking
running places a heavier demand on the heart within a short session
walking calls for a longer session to reach an equivalent result
each running stride drives a load through the joints above the person's own weight
follow-up surveys show that the gentler habit is given up less often
walking or exercise in a pool suits an affected joint better
the writer concludes that running yields more per session and walking more across a year
text: Does the heart need running, or will brisk walking do just as well? It depends on what you are after. Running works the heart muscle harder within a short session, while brisk walking asks for a far longer outing to reach anything comparable. The pounding on the ground, though, is another matter altogether. Every running stride drives a load through the joints well above the walker's own weight, which a gentler pace spares them. A second question follows: which of the two does anyone keep up? Follow-up surveys show that the less demanding habit is given up less often. Then comes the matter of a sore knee, or a hip that sets you limping. Caution leans towards walking, or towards exercise held up by water. The verdict stays balanced: running pays more per session, walking more across a year.

units: the chemist asks the customer when the fever began
the customer reports shivering that came on the evening before
she lists a sore throat, a running nose, sneezing and aching muscles
she admits to broken sleep and night sweats
the chemist picks out three priorities in what should be done
he says an ordinary medicine is enough against a troublesome fever
he puts making up the loss of water first
he sets difficulty in breathing as the signal to see a doctor
he recommends rest for as long as the muscles stay tender
text: The chemist asked the customer how long she had been feverish. She said the shivering had come on the evening before, out of nowhere. He wanted to know what else she felt. She listed a raw throat, a streaming nose, a constant urge to sneeze and aching calves. He then asked about her nights, and she admitted that she slept badly and woke up drenched. At that point the chemist set out three priorities. First the fever itself, which an ordinary medicine settles once it becomes a nuisance. Second, making up the water she was losing, which he put above everything else, since sweating drains the body. Third, keeping watch: should her breathing turn difficult, a doctor must be seen. The customer asked whether she ought to stop moving about. He advised rest for as long as the muscles stayed tender.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: surgeons once operated without cleaning their hands
a dirty operating apron was a matter of pride at the time
one stubborn doctor compared the death rate of two delivery wards
the death rate fell where hands were disinfected
his colleagues mocked him and he lost his post
work on micro-organisms brought his idea acceptance
sterilising instruments and airing rooms then spread widely
infections following operations dropped sharply
text: Picture a hospital where surgeons went from one bed to the next without so much as rinsing their hands, proud of the filth caked on their aprons. That was simply how things were done, and nobody saw any wrong in it. Then one stubborn doctor compared two delivery wards and noticed that deaths collapsed in the one where fingers were scrubbed with a biting solution. His colleagues laughed at him, and he ended up pushed out of his post. It took the work on micro-organisms before anyone would accept what he had shown. After that everything moved fast: instruments boiled, gowns changed, wards aired between operations. You know the rest. Infections following an operation fell away, and hand-washing turned into the cheapest and most rewarding gesture medicine has. Rather a funny turnaround, is it not?

units: sitting still for a long time makes the feet swell
the calf muscles push blood upwards by squeezing the veins
staying still halts that pumping action
fluid gathers in the tissue and presses on the nerves
that pressure on the nerves explains the prickling feeling
warmth adds to the effect by widening the vessels
a shortage of water thickens the blood and hinders the flow
the trouble normally clears after a night in a healthy adult
lasting stillness raises the risk of a clot forming
doctors advise standing up, tightening the calves, drinking and avoiding tight clothing
text: After a long journey spent sitting, the feet swell and the toes feel numb. The mechanism is well known to doctors. Blood climbs from the legs back to the heart because the calf muscles squeeze the veins at every step. Sit still and that pump stops. Fluid then gathers in the tissue, the foot puffs up, and the squeezed nerves send back a prickling feeling. Warmth makes it worse, since it widens the vessels. So does going short of water, because thicker blood travels less easily. In a healthy adult none of this amounts to much, and a night is enough to put it right. The danger grows, though, when the stillness drags on and a clot forms. Practitioners therefore advise standing up regularly, tightening the calves, drinking water and keeping clear of clothing that grips the waist.

units: a bookbinder stayed bent over her bench through long sessions
a dull ache spread through her forearm and then her fingers
she dropped her tool in the middle of a session
she ignored the symptom at first, thinking it would pass
the doctor she saw measured the height of the cutting surface instead of prescribing a remedy
the bench stood two hand-widths too low
the workshop was rearranged with a raised, tilted top and an adjustable seat
short breaks were brought in every half hour
the pain went within three weeks
text: The bookbinding workshop smelled of warm glue and damp paper. The binder stayed bent over her bench from dawn to dusk, wrist folded, jaw tight with concentration. A dull ache settled in her forearm, then crept into her fingers, until one afternoon her folding tool dropped out of her hand in the middle of a session. She put it down to a passing weakness and gritted her teeth. It got worse. A sports doctor, consulted with no real hope, prescribed neither ointment nor a long rest, but measured the height of the bench. Two hand-widths too low. The top was raised, the surface tilted, an adjustable stool brought in, and a short break set for every half hour. Within three weeks the pain had gone. She tells her apprentices the story laughing: her trouble came not from her hands but from her furniture.

units: the choice between a cold and a warm application depends on the nature of the injury
cold suits a recent injury with swelling
the ice pack must be kept off the skin by a cloth
the cold application alternates spells of a quarter of an hour
heat suits a long-standing stiffness without swelling
a warm bottle is laid on for half an hour
the time must be watched by the clock and stopped if the skin reddens deeply
cold soothes and tightens whereas heat relaxes and widens
in case of doubt cold carries fewer drawbacks
text: Before you reach for a compress, decide between cold and heat, because the two do quite different jobs. For a fresh injury, a joint that is puffing up or a knock taken the day before, choose cold. Wrap the pack in a thin cloth, hold it on for a quarter of an hour, take it off for as long again, then repeat. Never lay bare ice against the skin. For an old stiffness, a knotted neck or an aching muscle with no swelling, heat is the better choice. A warm bottle, left on for half an hour, loosens the fibres and makes movement easier. In either case, time it by the clock and stop if the skin turns deeply red. Hold on to the basic difference: cold soothes and tightens, heat relaxes and opens. When you cannot make up your mind, take the cold, whose drawbacks are the smaller ones.

units: a health survey carried out in a rural area identifies three areas of weakness
the diet of the adults questioned rests on soft, sugary food
poor chewing goes with damaged teeth from middle age
nights are short and broken by waking
lack of sleep tells on alertness at the wheel and on mood
motorised trips have displaced walking even over short distances
distance from care facilities is a factor common to all three
appointments are put off until the matter becomes urgent
the report calls for travelling surgeries, dental screening among children and waymarked paths
the health authorities will study these proposals before the end of the year
text: A health survey carried out across a rural district sets out three areas of weakness. The first is diet: the adults questioned eat soft, sugary food, chew little, and show damaged teeth from middle age onwards. The second concerns sleep. Nights there are short and broken by waking, which tells on alertness at the wheel and on temper. The third bears on physical activity, since walking has given way to motorised trips, even over short distances. The authors also note one factor running through all three, the distance to care. An appointment means a long journey, and many of them put it off until the matter is urgent. The report calls for travelling surgeries, dental screening among children and waymarked paths around the villages. The health authorities will look at these recommendations before the end of the year.
